On the evidence, the Panel found that, notwithstanding coronary bypass surgery in July 1987, the worker was totally disabled by his back condition during the period in question.  The appeal was allowed.  [5 pages]
The worker appealed a decision denying him entitlement for a right shoulder and arm disability which he claimed was related to his repetitive work on an automobile assembly line.

The worker had first been assessed for a 15% pension in 1988 under the interim policy for chronic pain disability.  The 15% pension was confirmed on reassessment under the Psychological and Behavioural Disorders Rating Schedule, which is now the rating schedule for fibromyalgia.

DecSummary: The worker suffered from carpal tunnel syndrome for which she was receiving a pension.  The Board originally also granted a pension for adhesive capsulitis of the right shoulder on the basis that it was related to the carpal tunnel syndrome.  The Board later reversed entitlement for the shoulder condition.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for the shoulder condition and denying temporary benefits for a period in 1988.

DecKeywords: Continuity (of treatment); Significant contribution (of employment to disability)
DecSummary: The worker suffered back injuries in March 1976, May 1977 and July 1978.  He experienced back pain while getting up at work in June 1980.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for two days in June 1980 and one day in July 1980.

He worked exclusively for one company that paid him a quoted price for each job.  Cost of materials was deducted from the fee.  On these facts, there is no dispute that the claimant would have been considered to be a deemed worker within the Board policy for construction workers.

The Panel found that at the time, the issues in dispute were initial and ongoing entitlement.  The Panel considered the appeal on this basis.  SIEF became an issue later but was not an issue at the time the Board made its determination.
Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer.  [4 pages]

DecKeywords: Temporary disability (beyond pension level); Temporary partial disability
DecSummary: The worker suffered knee injuries for which he was receiving a 23% pension.  He received temporary total disability benefits from March 1991 to September 1991 and 50% temporary partial disability benefits from September 1991 to November 1991.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying temporary total disability benefits from September to November.
Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer.  [3 pages]

DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision disqualifying him from receiving full benefits because he failed to accept suitable available employment.

The issue was whether the plaintiffs were in the course of employment at the time of the accident.
The worker was receiving a 15% pension for an organic disability and a 15% provisional award for a psychological disability.

The worker appealed a decision denying him benefits on the basis that he refused suitable work that was available at no wage loss.  The worker had epicondylitis of the left elbow and was awarded a 2% pension for that condition.  This condition is associated with, and perpetuated by, repetitive movements of the arm and wrist.
The worker fell and struck his head in February 1971.  The worker was appealing a decision of the Hearings Officer denying benefits for epilepsy.

The worker's request to reconsider Decision No. 61/92 was denied.  In Decision No. 61/92, the hearing panel denied the worker's request for a commutation for the purpose of starting a catering business.  The worker now wanted to establish a painting business.  This request was a new proposal which could be made directly to the Board.  [3 pages]

The worker injured his back in three industrial accidents that occurred in New Brunswick.  Those accidents  occurred in 1972, 1975, and 1980. The worker lost 65, 88 and 23 working days, respectively, as a result of those accidents.  In October 1982, the worker reported an accident while working in Ontario.  No time was lost as a result of this accident, but the worker was placed on modified duties and medical benefits were paid for chiropractic treatment.  The worker sought benefits for a back disability, for time lost after December 1982, that he claimed resulted from the 1982 Ontario accident.

DecKeywords: Chronic obstructive lung disease; Emphysema; Exposure (dust); Smoking; Mining (gold)
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision denying him benefits for chronic obstructive lung disease (COLD).  During his 30 years as an underground gold miner, he was exposed to considerable amounts of various types of dust, including aluminum dust.  The presence of dust in the worker's lungs was confirmed by biopsy.  It was agreed that the worker suffered from COLD, but there were only minor traces of silicosis which is recognized as a compensable industrial disease for gold miners.  The diagnosis of emphysema was confirmed in 1979.  Emphysema, which is an obstructive lung disease, is not a presumptively compensable condition for gold miners.

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement in 1978.  In accordance with Decision No. 65/92I, the Panel obtained further medical opinion regarding a relationship between surgery in 1978 and a compensable injury in 1975.  One report, based on more complete information than the doctor had previously, did not support a relationship.  A report from another doctor found no more than a possibility of a relationship.

DecKeywords: Apportionment; Discretion, Board (apportionment) (standard of review); Evidence (weight) (guilty plea); Negligence (occupiers' liability); Negligence (res ipsa loquitur)
DecSummary: The worker was a worker of a subcontractor at a construction site.  He was injured when some metal doors fell on him.  The doors had been piled on the floor by the contractor but had been moved without express permission of the contractor to a different location.  When moved, they were left leaning against a wall.  The contractor appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer transferring all of the costs of the accident from the subcontractor's cost record to the contractor's cost record.

DecKeywords: In the course of employment (travelling); Right to sue
DecSummary: The defendants in a civil case applied to determine whether the plaintiff's right of action was taken away.  The plaintiff was injured in a motor vehicle accident while proceeding home from a professional development seminar.  The seminar was held in a community about 200 kilometres from the plaintiff's home.  She was not required, but was expected, to attend.  She received a travel allowance and was compensated for the extra time spent at the seminar over that of her usual working hours.

DecKeywords: Access to worker file, statutory; Freedom of Information
DecSummary: Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer.  Disclosure under s. 71 of the Workers' Compensation Act does not contravene the provisions of the Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act.  [5 pages]

DecKeywords: Rehabilitation, vocational (program not offered by Board); Supplements, transitional provisions (temporary) (participation in rehabilitation)
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement to a supplement subsequent to March 1991.  In Decision No. 592/92I (February 16, 1993), the Panel found that the worker was entitled to further supplementary benefits.  The Panel referred the matter back to the Board for decision, after which the Panel would make a final decision.  The Board decided that the worker was entitled to a s. 147(2) supplement from March 1991 to October 1991, a s. 147(4) supplement from October 1991 to March 1993, and a s. 147(2) supplement subsequent to March 1993.

The worker, a construction labourer since 1956, injured his low back in three compensable accidents in 1978 and 1979.  He returned to his regular duties with no complaint after the first two accidents.  After the third injury there were occasional complaints of back pain, but in light of the absence of medical treatment, they did not establish an ongoing disability.

DecKeywords: In the course of employment (proceeding to and from work); Right to sue
DecSummary: The defendants in a civil case applied to determine whether the plaintiffs' right of action was taken away.  The issue was whether the parties were in the course of employment at the time of a motor vehicle accident.

DecKeywords: Leave to appeal (substantial new evidence) (subsequent Tribunal decision)
DecSummary: The worker applied for leave to appeal a decision of the Appeal Board denying entitlement for a back condition.  The worker suffered a right leg injury in 1971.  The Appeal Board found that shortening of the leg was insignificant and would not cause back problems.

The worker was struck on the left knee by a falling rock in 1980.  He did not report the accident for three days and did not seek medical treatment for one year.  There was a lack of treatment from 1981 until 1989, when the worker laid off due to knee pain.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement in 1989.

Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer, except for a number of references which were not relevant.  One document deleted by the Board had potential relevance and was released to the employer.  [4 pages]

The worker slipped in January 1990, injuring her low back and her knees.  She received temporary total disability benefits until January 1991.  In March 1991, she was awarded a 5% FEL award.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying temporary benefits from January 1991 to March 1991.

DecKeywords: Medical opinion (tear) (wrist) (triangular fibrocartilage complex); Preexisting condition (ulnar plus variant); Second Injury and Enhancement Fund {SIEF} (preexisting condition); Second Injury and Enhancement Fund {SIEF} (prolonged disability); Triangular fibrocartilage complex; Ulnar plus variant
DecSummary: The employer appealed a decision that the worker was entitled to continuing benefits after September 1989, when the worker unsuccessfully attempted to return to modified work.  In June 1989, the worker sustained an injury to his right forearm when he tried to catch a 90 pound plywood form to prevent it from falling.  His hand was bent backwards, causing immediate pain in his hand, wrist and forearm.

DecKeywords: Evidence (confidential information); Evidence (similar fact); Procedure (production of documents) (confidential information)
DecSummary: The worker was appealing denial of benefits for a stress-related emotional disability.  Her case focused on her relationship with her supervisor.  The worker sought access to the employer's personnel records which documented the supervisor's employment history.  She submitted that the documents may contain relevant evidence relating to her difficulties with the supervisor, or similar fact evidence revealing difficulties which other workers might have had with the supervisor.

DecKeywords: Accident (occurrence); Benefit of the doubt; Credibility; Delay (reporting injury)
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision denying him benefits for a knee disability.  He claimed that he was struck by a piece of scaffolding that fell while he was dismantling it.  The incident, which according to the worker occurred on August 22, was unwitnessed.  The worker's evidence was that he reported the incident and kept working despite his pain because the foreman told him that a claim form would be available on Friday, August 24.  The form was not made available by the employer on Friday.  On Monday, August 27 the worker sought medical treatment and it was clear that he was then suffering from a knee disability.  The employer submitted that the worker injured himself on the intervening weekend.

DecKeywords: Leave to appeal (good reason to doubt correctness) (Board procedure); Leave to appeal (good reason to doubt correctness) (consideration of evidence); Leave to appeal (substantial new evidence) (medical report)
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision of the WCB Appeal Board which held that his February 1979 compensable accident neither caused his back disability nor aggravated his preexisting degenerative disc disease, for the period subsequent to June 1981.  The Appeal Board found that there was no continuity of complaint between 1979 and 1981.  In this case, the WCB's second level of appeal (between the Decision Review Branch and the Appeal Board) was skipped for some reason.

DecKeywords: Suitable employment (suitable for worker's capabilities) (career change)
DecSummary: The worker, a press operator, sustained a repetitive strain injury to her left shoulder and neck.  She was receiving a 10% pension which was awarded under the Board's chronic pain disability guidelines, but which also included the organic aspects of her condition - cervical strain and rotator cuff tendonitis.

The worker suffered a hip injury in 1963 and low back injuries in 1973 and 1987.  The worker appealed denial of a pension for the hip injury, denial of continuing temporary benefits for the back injury after August 1989 and denial of an increase in the worker's 20% pension for low back disability.

The worker suffered a back injury in 1977 for which he was awarded a 20% pension.  He also received a wage loss supplement.  In 1986, the worker had a recurrence.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer regarding the earnings basis for calculation of benefits.

DecKeywords: Employer (definition of) (contract of hiring); In the course of employment (contemporaneity); In the course of employment (travelling); Right to sue (remoteness); Right to sue (workers of both employers)
DecSummary: The defendants in a civil case applied to determine whether the plaintiff's right of action was taken away.  The plaintiff was a travelling accountant.  Ninety-five per cent of his work involved travelling assignments.  The plaintiff attended the defendants' farm to do some accounting work.  He slipped on ice while proceeding to his car after finishing his work.  The defendants' farming operation did not require daily attention.  Chores were done by the defendants themselves or by three nephews who were called from time to time to help.  No work had been done by the nephews for about 10 days prior to the accident.

DecKeywords: Board Directives and Guidelines (in the course of employment) (plazas and malls); In the course of employment (plazas and malls); In the course of employment (proceeding to and from work); Right to sue
DecSummary: The defendant in a civil case applied to determine whether the plaintiff's right of action was taken away.  The worker worked in a department store located in an enclosed shopping centre.  She slipped and fell in the enclosed portion of the mall while proceeding to the employees' entrance to the department store.  The accident occurred shortly after 9 o'clock in the morning.  The plaintiff did not begin work until 10:30 but it was her regular practice to arrive early, do some preparatory work and then do some shopping in the mall.  The plaintiff brought an action against the owner of the mall.  The issue was whether the plaintiff was in the course of employment at the time of the accident.

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a back condition.  The worker claimed that she felt pain in her back while attempting to open a window at work.  Two days later she suffered a severe pain at home while bending to pick up a cushion.

The worker suffered a shoulder strain in May 1988.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a back injury which the worker claimed she also suffered in the accident and denying continuing entitlement subsequent to November 1988.

DecKeywords: Supplements, transitional provisions (benefit from rehabilitation); Supplements, transitional provisions (rehabilitation) (cooperation)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a low back injury in 1967 for which he was awarded a 10% pension in 1970, increased over the years to 45% in 1986.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying a supplement under s. 147(4).

The worker suffered a low back injury in January 1986 and received benefits until February 1986.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying further entitlement in July 1988.  On the evidence, the Panel found that the worker's condition in 1988 was not a recurrence of the compensable condition.  Rather, it was the result of the natural progression of preexisting degenerative disc disease.  The appeal was dismissed.  [8 pages]
The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer confirming a 15% pension for chronic pain.

DecKeywords: Administrative Fund (transfer of costs); Suitable employment; Availability for employment (reassessment of negative decision)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a compensable injury in 1987.  He had a recurrence in June 1989, leading to a brief lay-off.  In July 1989, the worker refused a job with the employer that was outside the bargaining unit.  This job was suitable for the worker and the refusal was based on poor advice.  The worker's benefits were reduced to temporary partial difference benefits.  The worker appealed denial of full benefits from September 1989 to February 1991.

DecKeywords: Adjournment (conflict of interest); Right to sue; Withdrawal (of application)
DecSummary: A s. 17 application was considered by the Panel to be withdrawn.  It was apparent to the Panel that the applicants were not prepared to proceed for reasons which were unclear but which related to evidentiary difficulties and conflicts relating to carriage of the application.  The applicants requested an adjournment, but this was refused by the Panel due to inconsequent or incomprehensible argument.  In the circumstances, the Panel considered it more appropriate to consider the application withdrawn.  [11 pages]

DecKeywords: In the course of employment (travelling); Right to sue (workers of both employers)
DecSummary: This section 17 application arose out of a motor vehicle collision between a vehicle occupied by the plaintiffs and a vehicle operated by the defendant.  The plaintiffs were bakery managers for separate stores in the same grocery store chain.  They were on their way to attend the chain's annual meeting for bakery managers and supervisors at the time of the accident.  They were workers of a Schedule 1 employer.  The defendant was an executive officer of a sole proprietorship reporting to the Board as a Schedule 1 industry.  He had not elected to have personal coverage under the Act.

The worker suffered a twisting injury to his foot in October 1986, for which he did not lose any time.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement from May 1989 to September 1989.

The worker was appealing denial of temporary benefits for a specific period.  The worker had two compensable accidents with different employers.  One of the employers had only received about three weeks notice of the hearing.  The hearing was adjourned to allow that employer to obtain representation.  [4 pages]

DecKeywords: Medical report (payment for); Travel expenses (to hearing)
DecSummary: In an addendum, the Panel dealt with the worker's request for payment of expenses.  The Panel directed payment for a medical report and noise level surveys.  These were evidentiary matters which were probative to the issue in dispute.

DecSummary: The plaintiffs in a civil case applied to determine whether their right of action was taken away.  The plaintiffs were the wife and children of C, who died in a motor vehicle accident.  The defendants were the driver of the other vehicle, and the owners of the tractor and trailer that was being driven by the defendant driver.  The issues were whether C was a worker at the time of the accident and, if so, whether he was in the course of employment and, if so, whether the defendant driver was a worker of a Schedule 1 employer.

DecKeywords: Rehabilitation, vocational (eligibility); Supplements, transitional provisions (benefit from rehabilitation); Supplements, transitional provisions (temporary)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a knee injury in 1981 for which he was awarded a 12% pension.  He also received a temporary supplement under s. 43(5) of the pre-1985 Act.  The worker completed a Board approved retraining programme at a community college in June 1989.  He was awarded a temporary supplement under s. 135(2) of the pre-1990 Act from July 1989 to June 1990.  At that point he was awarded a permanent supplement under s. 135(4).  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying further entitlement to a supplement under s. 135(2).

DecKeywords: In the course of employment (proceeding to and from work) (employer's vehicle); Jurisdiction, Tribunal (right to sue) (member of the family); Right to sue; Words and phrases (while in the employment)
DecSummary: The defendant in a civil case applied to determine whether the plaintiff's right of action was taken away.  The plaintiff was the cook in the defendant's restaurant.  It was the usual practice for the defendant to give the plaintiff a ride home from the restaurant in Mississauga to the area where both the plaintiff and defendant lived in downtown Toronto at the end of the work day.  The defendant was involved in a motor vehicle accident at about 3:30 in the morning as he was driving home.  The issue was whether the plaintiff was in the course of employment at the time of the accident.

DecKeywords: Availability for employment (job search); Rehabilitation, vocational (cooperation)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a low back injury in October 1985.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer granting 50% benefits from September 1986 to December 1986.
The worker suffered a serious low back injury in 1966 for which he was awarded a 30% pension.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a cervical condition.

The worker suffered a right elbow and shoulder injury in January 1990.  He returned to modified work in March 1990 and worked until April 1990.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying benefits subsequent to April 1990.
The hearing was adjourned to allow the worker to obtain a representative.  The worker thought he was represented by a paralegal service but no one came to attend the hearing.  [3 pages]

DecKeywords: Suitable employment; Temporary partial disability (level of benefits)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a bilateral wrist disability from the nature of her work in November 1988.  She received temporary benefits until October 1990 when she refused work which the Board found to be suitable.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying temporary benefits subsequent to October 1990.

DecKeywords: Aggravation (preexisting condition) (vascular disease); Board Directives and Guidelines (cardiac conditions); Health care (medical aid) (drugs); Heart attack
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision denying him health care benefits beyond the date of the Hearings Officer decision in June 1991.  The health care benefits in issue were paid to reimburse the worker for drugs that he was taking.  The worker sustained a compensable myocardial infarction in April 1985.  In June 1985 he underwent quintuple bypass surgery.  The worker had asymptomatic underlying coronary disease preceding the work injury.  He would not have been considered to have a 'heart condition' prior to the April 1985 infarct.  He was currently receiving a 40% pension for his heart condition.

DecKeywords: Agreement (parties); Board Directives and Guidelines (re-employment) (voluntary severance); Re-employment (termination); Waiver (right to compensation); Withdrawal (of appeal)
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision of the Reinstatement Officer finding that the employer did not breach its re-employment obligations.  After the hearing of the worker's evidence, the parties reached a settlement proposal.  The Panel was not informed of the details.

DecKeywords: Disability (disabled from working); Hypertension; Pensions (Rating Schedule) (chronic pain)
DecSummary: The worker injured his back in 1973.  In 1976, he was granted a 10% pension that was increased to 15% in 1981.  The worker stopped working in 1979.  After that date, he periodically received temporary disability benefits, but all of his attempts at returning to work were unsuccessful. In 1979 the worker started receiving treatment for hypertension (high blood pressure).  The Board accepted that the worker suffered from a chronic pain disability and that the worker's hypertension was compensable because it was aggravated by the work injury.

The employer was appealing a decision of the Reinstatement Officer finding that the employer had failed to fulfil its obligations under s. 54 and assessing a penalty.  The employer wanted to appeal at this time only on the issue of whether the worker had made a timely application to the Board.

DecKeywords: Merits and justice; Notice of hearing; Three week rule (documents); Three week rule (witnesses)
DecSummary: The worker was injured at work in September 1983. He claimed that he suffered groin and low back injuries in that accident. The worker had back problems relating, at least in part, to a prior compensable accident.
The appeal was withdrawn to allow the worker to pursue further issues at the Board.  [3 pages]

The worker suffered an injury in March 1990.  The employer's report of the accident showed an income tax exemption code 01, meaning that the worker had no dependants.  The worker completed a form in November 1990 stating a correct tax code 02, meaning that the worker had dependants.  The Board adjusted the tax code effective January 1991.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer refusing to adjust the tax code back to the date of the accident.

The appeal was withdrawn to allow the worker to pursue entitlement at the Board for non-organic disability.  If the worker returns to the Tribunal, the matter could then be considered on a whole person basis.  [4 pages]

The employer's request to reconsider Decision No. 571/92 was denied.  In Decision No. 571/92, the hearing panel granted temporary benefits for a new accident to a worker who was already in receipt of a pension.

DecKeywords: Leave to appeal (good reason to doubt correctness) (consideration of evidence); Leave to appeal (substantial new evidence) (documents)
DecSummary: The worker's widow applied for leave to appeal a decision of the Appeal Board denying dependency benefits for the worker's death from lung cancer.

DecKeywords: Pensions (assessment) (back); Pensions (assessment) (psychotraumatic disability); Pensions (assessment) (whole person concept)
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer confirming the worker's pension.  The worker was receiving a 40% pension for organic disability and a 20% pension for non-organic disability.

The hearing of the worker's appeal was adjourned due to the absence of the worker.  This was the second time the worker had failed to appear for a hearing.  His absence may have been due to memory loss which he claimed was caused by exposure at work to various solvents.  The Panel recommended to the worker's representative that she take steps to ensure the attendance of the worker at the next hearing.  [4 pages]

DecKeywords: Second Injury and Enhancement Fund {SIEF} (preexisting condition)
DecSummary: The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying SIEF relief.  The worker slipped and fell at work, bumping his head and injuring his shoulder.  On the evidence, the Panel found that the worker had peripheral neuropathy and periarthritis which preexisted the accident and which prolonged or enhanced the disability.  The worker was also obese and had diabetes.  These were also significant preexisting conditions which affected his ability to return to work.

The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer granting entitlement for a low back disability resulting from strenuous work in July 1989.  The worker had previous back injuries in 1970, 1981 and 1985.  However, the worker's reporting of the accident in 1989 and the medical evidence indicated that the worker had an acute injury in 1989 and that the worker's work was a significant contributing factor to the injury.
Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer.  [4 pages]

DecKeywords: Adjournment (Board submissions); Apportionment (industrial disease) (hearing loss); Tinnitus; Hearing loss; Industrial disease (out of province exposure); Interjurisdictional agreements (industrial disease)
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer confirming entitlement for hearing loss from noise exposure but restricting benefits to health care only.  The Hearings Officer found that the worker qualified for a 1% pension but was not entitled to the pension since the majority of exposure occurred in Manitoba.  The Hearings Officer also denied benefits for tinnitus because of the out-of-province exposure.

The worker suffered a left hip and leg injury in April 1984.  He received benefits until June 1984 when he was cleared to return to work.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying further benefits.

The worker fell at work in December 1980.  She appealed an award of 50% temporary partial disability benefits from September 1981 to June 1984 and of 75% temporary partial disability benefits from September 1985 to May 1988.  She claimed entitlement to full benefits for both periods.

The worker suffered a knee sprain in May 1973 but did not lose any time.  In 1989, the worker underwent knee replacement surgery.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying ongoing entitlement.  The Hearings Officer found that the 1973 accident was an aggravation of a preexisting osteoarthritic condition and the worker's condition returned to its pre-accident state within one year of the accident.

The worker suffered a right shoulder injury in February 1989.  She was discharged from HRC to modified work in April 1990.  She returned to modified work with no wage loss in April 1990 but laid off after four hours.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying temporary benefits subsequent to April 1990.
The employer was allowed to withdraw its appeal in order to obtain representation.  [3 pages]

The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer granting entitlement for aggravation of preexisting cervical degenerative disc disease.  The Panel found that the worker's job was repetitive and, although not specifically requiring neck movement, would involve at least slight rotation of the neck.  The work aggravated underlying degenerative disc disease.

The worker's widow appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying survivor benefits for the 33 year old worker's death by suicide.  The worker was a self-employed wood cutter and skidder.  He suffered a severe low back strain in April 1984.  The Board denied initial entitlement until March 1987 when the Board decision was reversed by the Tribunal.

DecKeywords: Accident (occurrence); Benefit of the doubt; Chance event
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision denying her entitlement for a knee condition diagnosed as pre-patellar bursitis.  The worker claimed that she banged her knees on the floor at work on December 20, 1988.  Neither the report of the employer's first aid attendant nor the employer's report to the Board referred to a specific accident that day.  The worker saw a doctor shortly after the alleged accident, but his report did not refer to a specific work accident.  When the worker described her accident history to the Board in February 1989, she did not relate her problems to a specific blow to her knees.  The worker testified that she told the employer, the Board and all her doctors the full details of her accident.

DecKeywords: Consequences of injury (altered gait); Fracture (knee) (osteochondral); Preexisting condition (gonnococcal infection)
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision denying benefits for his right and left knee disabilities.  His job as a cutter in the bush involved walking over uneven terrain and kneeling on the gound on a regular basis.  The worker fell, banging his left knee against tree stumps, in September 1983 and in January 1985.  Medical treatment was received for both incidents, but no time was lost from work.

DecKeywords: Impairment of earning capacity; Significantly greater than is usual; Supplements, temporary
DecSummary: The worker suffered a low back injury in 1981 for which he was awarded a 15% pension.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying a temporary supplement from September 1983 to September 1985.

DecSummary: The worker suffered a low back injury in April 1986.  He returned to modified work in May 1989 but stopped working after one week.  The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer granting full benefits subsequent to May 1989 and denying SIEF relief to the employer.

DecKeywords: Carpal tunnel syndrome; Delay (onset of symptoms)
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for carpal tunnel syndrome which the worker related to his work as a welder.  The worker did not claim benefits until 14 years after his retirement.  The condition was in his non-dominant hand.  Further, he was able to continue with activities, such as playing the cello, in the years after his retirement.

DecKeywords: Penalties; Board Directives and Guidelines (penalty assessments) (distortions)
DecSummary: The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer confirming a penalty assessment for the years 1987-89.

DecSummary: An underground miner appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for hearing loss and tinnitus related to noise exposure at work from 1964 to 1974.

The source of the alleged noise was a printing press 20 feet away from the worker's station.  The worker worked 17 hours per week, but would only be exposed to printing press noise one hour per day.

The employer submitted that it was requesting the examination under terms of a collective agreement and that s. 23 did not apply since this was not a case of a worker who 'has made a claim for compensation' as required by s. 23(1).
Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer, except for a reference which was not relevant.  [4 pages]

DecKeywords: Temporary partial disability; Temporary total disability
DecSummary: The worker suffered a low back injury in 1981.  She suffered a recurrence in February 1988 and received temporary total disability benefits until June 1989 and temporary partial disability benefits at the 50% rate from June 1989 to February 1991.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying temporary total disability benefits subsequent to June 1989.

The worker suffered a compensable foot injury in 1963 for which he was awarded a 15% pension.  A number of commutation requests by the worker were denied by the Board.  In 1970, the Board commuted the worker's pension unilaterally.  In 1979, the Board denied the worker's request to reconstitute his pension.  In 1991, the worker appealed to the Hearings Officer.  The worker appealed the decision of the Hearings Officer refusing to reconstitute the pension.

DecKeywords: Accident (occurrence); Adjournment (representation) (adequacy); Aggravation (preexisting condition) (disc, degeneration); Chance event; Presumptions (entitlement)
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a neck and low back condition.  The hearing was adjourned on the first day of the hearing because the Panel felt that the worker's representative was not prepared.  The Panel directed Tribunal counsel to forward to the representative Tribunal decisions on the issues in the appeal and, if necessary, to be present at the reconvened hearing to raise supplementary questions.
The worker, age 91 at the time of the hearing, appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for hearing loss, which the worker attributed to a fall of eight feet in February 1957.

The worker was struck on the side of the head on March 4, 1989.  He returned to work the following day.  He laid off again on March 28, 1989, due to a neck condition, diagnosed as cervical radiculopathy.  The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer granting benefits for the lay-off on March 28.

DecKeywords: Chronic pain; Hearing loss (traumatic); Referral to Board
DecSummary: The worker was injured in 1980 when he fell from a ladder.  In 1985, he was awarded a 15% pension for low back disability and a 15% pension for psychotraumatic disability.  The worker appealed denial of entitlement for hearing loss in one ear, denial of entitlement for chronic pain and confirmation of the pensions.

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for an arm injury.  The Panel found the worker to be a credible witness.  Considering the evidence of the worker and the other witnesses, the Panel found that the worker fell at work and injured her arm.

The worker suffered injuries for which he was awarded a 7.5% pension in 1987.  In 1990, the pension was increased to 17.5%.  From March 1989 to May 1989, the worker received temporary benefits at the 50% rate.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying temporary total disability benefits from March to May 1989.

The worker was receiving a 25% pension for a low back disability with left leg and foot involvement.  In March 1987, he sustained another compensable accident and temporary total benefits were paid until December 1987.  The worker and the employer agreed that the worker was totally disabled after December 1987, but disagreed as to the reason why.  The worker claimed that it was because of right lower leg and back pain.  The employer argued that the worker's back condition had reverted to its 25% pension level and that the continuing disability was because of a pre-existing shoulder condition.

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying a commutation of the worker's pension, valued at about $62,000, for the purpose of buying a dump truck and setting up a business driving the truck.

DecKeywords: Penalties; Board Directives and Guidelines (penalty assessments) (improved record)
DecSummary: The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer confirming a penalty assessment for the years 1986-88.
The worker's request to reconsider Decision No. 237/92 was denied.
The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying commutation of his pension, valued at about $80,000.  The worker wanted the commutation for the purpose of opening a service station.

The worker suffered a compensable head and shoulder injury in August 1986 and a rib injury in April 1987.  He did not immediately lose any time for these injuries.  In July 1987, he suffered a non-compensable low back injury.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a mid-back condition.
The worker suffered low back injuries in 1975 and 1977 and a shoulder injury in 1980.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement in 1981.

DecKeywords: Presumptions (termination of re-employment) (burden of proof); Re-employment (termination)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a compensable injury on October 16, 1990, and returned to work on October 23.  His employment was terminated on October 25.  The worker appealed a decision of the Reinstatement Officer finding that the employer did not breach its re-employment obligations.

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer confirming a 20% pension for back disability and denying a pension for hip disability.  In Decision No. 176/92I, the Panel found that the worker was not entitled to a pension for the hip disability and referred the worker back to the Board for reassessment of the pension for back disability.  On the reassessment, the Board found that the 20% award was adequate.

DecKeywords: Permanent disability (retroactive adjudication); Temporary disability (beyond pension level)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a compensable shoulder injury in 1985 for which he underwent surgery in 1987.  He laid off again in April 1988.  In June 1988, he suffered a non-compensable heart attack.  In January 1989, he was awarded a 23% pension for the shoulder disability retroactive to 1987.  In February 1989, he took early retirement.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying temporary benefits from April 1988 to February 1989.

The worker suffered a non-compensable back injury in 1976, for which he underwent surgery in 1977.  He suffered a compensable back injury in September 1981 and received benefits until he returned to work in March 1982.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a lay-off in 1983.

DecKeywords: Board Directives and Guidelines (SIEF) (recurrences); Second Injury and Enhancement Fund {SIEF} (recurrences)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a wrist injury in September 1989.  He returned to work with the accident employer on a work trial in August 1990,  but laid off again after a few days due to increased pain.  The Board granted benefits to the worker in August 1990 for a recurrence.  The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying SIEF relief.

The worker twisted her back at work in June 1987.  It was determined that she was fit for modified duties in January 1987.  The worker attempted to return to light work in February 1987, but was unable to work for more than a few hours due to back pain.  The worker appealed a decision denying her entitlement to total temporary benefits after January 1987.
The hearing was adjourned to allow the worker to pursue entitlement for non-organic disability at the Board.  [4 pages]
The appeal was considered withdrawn due to the absence of the worker, who had forgotten about the hearing, despite having spoken to his representative two days before the scheduled date.  [3 pages]

DecKeywords: Rehabilitation, vocational (eligibility); Supplements, transitional provisions (benefit from rehabilitation); Supplements, transitional provisions (increase in earning capacity)
DecSummary: A construction worker suffered a back injury in 1980, for which he was awarded a 15% pension.  As a result of a job placement by his Rehabilitation Counsellor, he began work as a car park attendant in December 1988.  He suffered a recurrence in 1990 and was not rehired when he was capable of working again.  The worker was granted a s. 135(4) supplement.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying a s. 135(2) supplement.

The worker appealed the denial of a s. 147(2) temporary supplement.  The worker was injured in 1982.  He returned to work, but had suffered a number of recurrences.  He was awarded a 15% pension in 1984, increased to 20% in 1990.  While he was off work due to his latest recurrence, which occurred in September 1989, the worker became involved in a dispute with a supervisor.  As a result of this incident the worker was given the choice of resigning and receiving a settlement from the accident employer, or being fired upon returning to work (subject to the grievance procedure in a collective agreement).  He chose to resign in August 1990.

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a respiratory condition.  The worker worked as a construction labourer building tunnels.  He worked for one employer from 1967 to 1981 in very dusty conditions.  He worked for a second employer from 1981 to 1987 in better conditions.  The worker became acutely ill in 1987.  His condition was diagnosed as chronic bronchitis.

DecKeywords: Supplements, transitional provisions (benefit from rehabilitation); Supplements, transitional provisions (permanent); Supplements, transitional provisions (temporary)
DecSummary: The worker was injured in 1980 and was receiving a pension.  He last worked in April 1985.  The worker was in receipt of full benefits in one form or another from April 1985 to February 1988, including temporary supplements for some of that period.  In February 1988, the worker's temporary supplement was terminated on the basis that he was not co-operating in his vocational rehabilitation program.  The full temporary supplement was restored in November 1988 and paid until February 1990, at which time it was reduced to the permanent supplement available under s. 147(4)

DecKeywords: Availability for employment; Re-employment (non-compliance) (mitigation by worker); Re-employment (non-compliance) (payments)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a low back strain in June 1991. The employer did not re-employ the worker.  The Reinstatement Officer found that the employer had breached its re-employment obligations under s. 54 and assessed a penalty of $1,000.  The Reinstatement Officer also awarded the worker the equivalent of temporary partial disability benefits for a period of one month.  The worker appealed regarding the length of benefits.

The worker suffered a back injury at work in 1974.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying further entitlement in 1986.  The Panel found that the worker was not entitled to further benefits.  She recovered from the compensable accident.  Her condition was likely related to non-compensable preexisting scoliosis.  The appeal was dismissed.  [8 pages]

The worker was not entitled to benefits for a back disability.  The worker became ill and left work on March 15, 1990.  However, she did not report back pain to her manager or on her admission to hospital that day.  When she contacted her employer some days later, she made no mention of a work-related back disability and asked to use her vacation time as sick leave, due to a prior non-compensable illness.  There was no evidence of any specific physical event involving the worker's back that day.  [7 pages]

The worker suffered compensable low back injuries in August 1977 and September 1978.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for chronic pain.  On the evidence, the worker was suffering from chronic pain related to the compensable accidents.  The worker was entitled to a pension retroactive to May 27, 1986.  The appeal was allowed.  [12 pages]
The worker suffered a back injury in September 1989.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for chronic pain.

DecKeywords: Board Directives and Guidelines (tinnitus); Tinnitus; Health care (appliances or apparatus) (hearing aid); Hearing loss
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for hearing loss and tinnitus.  The Hearings Officer found that, although the worker was exposed to noise, the loss was not sufficient to warrant health care benefits or a pension and that, since the worker was not entitled to benefits for hearing loss, he was also not entitled to benefits for tinnitus.

DecKeywords: In the course of employment (fighting); In the course of employment (residential employees)
DecSummary: The worker was injured in an altercation with a co-worker.  The worker was a cook in an isolated location in northern Ontario.  The worker and co-worker were both living in the staff quarters provided by the employer.  The altercation took place during non-working hours.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement.
The appeal was withdrawn to allow the worker to pursue additional issues at the Board.  [4 pages]

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for hearing loss.  The Hearings Officer found that, although the worker was exposed to noise, his hearing loss was not compatible with noise induced hearing loss.

DecKeywords: In the course of employment (proceeding to and from work) (employer's vehicle); Right to sue
DecSummary: The defendants in a civil action applied to determine whether the plaintiff's right of action was taken away.  The issue was whether the plaintiff was in the course of employment at the time of a motor vehicle accident.

DecKeywords: Board Directives and Guidelines (health care) (independent living); Health care (home modification); Health care (snow blower); Health care (tractor lawnmower); Rehabilitation (lessening handicap)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a severe right foot injury in 1977, resulting in amputation of his foot above the ankle.  Later, he developed a left knee disability as a consequence of overuse.  He was awarded a pension of 37%.  The Board paid for prostheses as needed, including a swim leg and a sports leg.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying reimbursement for the cost of a snow blower and a tractor lawnmower.

The worker suffered a shoulder sprain in August 1989 and was off work for one week.  On November 8, 1989, the employer gave the worker two weeks notice that her employment was being terminated for excessive absenteeism.  On November 16, 1989, the worker claimed a recurrence of the compensable injury.  The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer granting ongoing benefits for right shoulder disability.

DecKeywords: Board Directives and Guidelines (construction industry worker); Independent operator (construction); Worker (deemed)
DecSummary: The issue was whether the claimant for benefits was a worker within the meaning of the Act.  The claimant was a roofer.  He was working on his sixth roofing job for the alleged accident employer when he was injured.
Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer.  [3 pages]
Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer.  [3 pages]

DecKeywords: Disablement (awkward position); Disc, degeneration (cervical); Disc, herniated (cervical)
DecSummary: The worker was an underground miner who operated heavy equipment, particularly a bulldozer, from 1986 to 1988.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for cervical degenerative disc disease and a herniated disc.
Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer.  [3 pages]

DecKeywords: Access to worker file, statutory (deletion of material)
DecSummary: Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer, except for one sentence which the Board deleted and which the Panel agreed was not relevant to the issue in dispute of continuing entitlement for a knee disability.  The sentence referred to a minor non-compensable condition which was not related to the knee disability.  There was no reason to conclude that there was a psychological condition which could make relevant the worker's entire health status.  [4 pages]
Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer, except for a number of references which were not relevant.  [3 pages]
The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for tinnitus in 1986 which the worker related to noise exposure at work or to a fall in March 1984.

Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer, including a medical report that the Board did not release.  The employer claimed that the worker was not entitled to further benefits for a right knee condition.  The report in question dealt with the left knee.  The report was relevant since it shed light on the history of the worker's knee disability.  [3 pages]

DecKeywords: Access to worker file, statutory (issue in dispute) (relevance) (subsequent periods)
DecSummary: Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer, except for medical records dated after the date of the Board decision which was in dispute.  [6 pages]
Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer.  [3 pages]
The worker fractured two fingers in a compensable accident in 1968.  In 1982, he was awarded a 3% pension.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer confirming the pension.

DecKeywords: Impairment of earning capacity (minimal impairment); Issue setting; Permanent disability; Significantly greater than is usual; Supplements, temporary
DecSummary: The worker suffered a back injury in January 1980.  On a pension assessment in 1982, he was found to be fit to perform his regular work.  His permanent disability award was 0%.  He returned to the accident employer in November 1982 but, on the advice of the company doctor, the employer refused to re-employ the worker.  A grievance filed by the worker was dismissed, the arbitrator finding that the employer was justified in its actions.  The worker claimed that he continued to experience back problems and appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying a temporary supplement.

The worker was injured at work on May 28, 1989.  He sought medical attention on May 31 and tendonitis of the wrist was diagnosed.  He attempted to return to work on June 20, 1989 but had to stop working on June 28 because of symptoms affecting his wrist, neck and shoulder.  Benefits were paid for the first period of wrist disability, but were denied for the shoulder and neck disability after June 28.
A hearing was scheduled for December 10.  The Tribunal was advised on December 4 that the employer had health problems.  On consent, the hearing was adjourned.  [3 pages]

The worker suffered a low back injury in June 1987.  He returned to modified work in May 1990 but laid off after three days due to aggravation of his condition.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying full benefits subsequent to May 1990.

The employer was appealing a decision granting benefits to the worker's widow for the worker's lung cancer.  After the hearing was commenced and recessed for further investigation, the employer notified the Tribunal that it wanted to withdraw the appeal.

DecKeywords: Board Directives and Guidelines (supplements, temporary) (policy change); Merits and justice; Supplements, transitional provisions (temporary)
DecSummary: The worker injured his shoulder and upper back in 1983.  He was awarded a 13% pension in 1987.  The worker was receiving supplementary benefits under s. 45(5) of the pre-1989 Act.  On July 10, 1989 he began a training course, but he had to leave on July 12 because of neck pain.  The worker's rehabilitation file was closed.  As the classroom activity aggravated the worker's condition beyond his pension level, he was granted total disability benefits from July 13, 1989 to November 29, 1989 when his disability returned to his pension level.  His rehabilitation file was re-opened in March 1990.  The issue was the worker's entitlement to a supplement from November 1989 to March 1990.

DecKeywords: Hearing loss; Medical opinion (hearing loss) (deterioration after removal from exposure)
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for hearing loss.  When the worker stopped working in 1983, he had hearing loss of 25 decibels in one ear and 15 decibels in the other.  This was not enough for entitlement.  His hearing deteriorated after he stopped working and was no longer exposed to noise.  The Panel accepted medical opinion that noise induced hearing loss should not continue to deteriorate after removal from exposure.

The worker's request to reconsider Decision No. 168/92 was denied.  In Decision No. 168/92, the hearing panel denied the worker's request for interest and costs.  There was no reason to interfere with the hearing panel's decision.  [4 pages]

DecKeywords: In the course of employment (personal activity); Right to sue; Three week rule (witnesses) (summary of evidence); Travel expenses (to hearing)
DecSummary: The defendants in a civil case applied to determine whether the plaintiff's right of action was taken away.  The issue was whether the plaintiff and the defendant driver were in the course of employment at the time of a single vehicle accident.

DecKeywords: In the course of employment (benefit to the employer); In the course of employment (proceeding to and from work) (employer's vehicle); Right to sue
DecSummary: The defendants in a civil action applied to determine whether the plaintiff's right of action was taken away.  The issue considered in this decision was whether the plaintiff was in the course of employment at the time of a motor vehicle accident.  It was not necessary to consider a number of other issues.

DecKeywords: Agreement (parties); Board Directives and Guidelines (re-employment) (voluntary severance); Evidence (admissibility) (settlement); Re-employment (non-compliance) (penalty); Waiver (right to compensation)
DecSummary: The Reinstatement Officer found that the employer failed to fulfil its obligations under s. 54 of the Act and awarded the worker full benefits for a specific period and levied a penalty against the employer.  The employer appealed the decision of the Reinstatement Officer, originally on the basis of the finding that the employer failed to fulfil its obligations.  However, at the hearing, the employer asked the Panel to restrict the appeal to the penalty.  The worker supported the employer in asking for waiver of the penalty.  This was in accordance with minutes of settlement agreed to between the parties.
The hearing of an employer assessment appeal was adjourned to allow the employer to try to obtain more evidence as to allocation of workers' time between different functions.  [3 pages]

The worker suffered a head injury when he fell at work.  He was awarded a 3% pension for anosmia (loss of taste and smell).  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement to a pension for headaches also resulting from the accident.

The worker appealed a decision that found no relationship between her low back condition and her employment.  She had performed the same job since 1976.  The worker stated that she began to experience constant pain in her back in 1981, but that the pain was manageable.  In January 1986 the condition began to deteriorate and she was forced to stop working in September 1986.

After a preliminary hearing, a further hearing was scheduled to hear evidence of the worker and legal submissions.  Two days before the scheduled date to reconvene, the worker's representative informed the Tribunal that the worker would not be able to attend.  The worker was a truck driver and was in California for a delivery and would not be back in time for the hearing.  The employer did not object to the adjournment.

DecKeywords: Suitable employment; Benefit of the doubt; Credibility
DecSummary: The employer appealed a decision, granting the worker continuing entitlement to temporary total benefits for a knee disability, on the basis that the worker failed to accept available and suitable employment.  The work offered involved cleaning steel plates.  The worker claimed that the work was unsuitable because he was required to perform it standing up and he had to step over beams lying on the floor.

The employer's request, that the worker attend for an examination at a doctor of the employer's choosing, was denied.  The employer's intention to appeal initial entitlement for the worker's carpal tunnel syndrome condition and to apply for SIEF relief were valid compensation goals, but the examination was not important to the achievement of those goals.

DecKeywords: Medical examination (employer request); Procedure (medical examination) (employer request) (access to worker file)
DecSummary: The worker objected to the employer's request that the worker attend, on January 20, 1992, to be examined by a doctor chosen by the employer.  The worker was injured on December 6, 1991.  The worker's doctor filled out occupational fitness assessment forms provided by the employer.  The worker returned to modified duties, four hours per day, on January 28, 1992.

The worker suffered a low back injury in February 1990.  After discharge from HRC with medical restrictions, the worker returned to a two week work trial followed by a transitional work programme, arranged by the worker's rehabilitation counsellor.  The worker stopped work during the transitional programme in February 1991.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer finding that the work was suitable.

DecKeywords: Adjournment (additional evidence); Investigation by Tribunal; Procedure (absent parties); Right to sue
DecSummary: The defendant applicants did not appear at the hearing of a s. 17 application.  The representatives of the applicants and respondents had agreed prior to the hearing not to call witnesses but, rather, to rely on transcripts of examinations for discovery.
Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer.  [4 pages]

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a back disability.  The worker had a preexisting back condition.  She experienced a sharp stab of pain at the beginning of her shift while sitting and reaching forward for some paperwork.  The Panel found that employment was not a significant contributing factor to the disability.  Rather, the symptoms were evidence of the disabling nature of the preexisting condition.

DecKeywords: Credibility; Significant contribution (of employment to disability)
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a shoulder condition.  The Panel found the worker's evidence unreliable, particularly in regard to his failure to inform the Claims Adjudicator of prior similar complaints.  The worker had symptoms that were increasing over time to the point where he informed his employer of the pain.  It was not established the work was a significant contributing factor to the worker's disability.  The appeal was dismissed.  [10 pages]

DecKeywords: Suitable employment; Maximal medical rehabilitation; Pensions (arrears); Rehabilitation, vocational (cooperation); Supplements, temporary (wage loss); Supplements, transitional provisions (benefit from rehabilitation)
DecSummary: The worker sustained injuries to his shoulder and back in compensable accidents in 1980, 1981 and April 1984. Following the 1984 accident, the worker received temporary total disability benefits from April 1984 to August 1984 and from February 1986 to October 1987.  In 1987 he was awarded pensions that were effective as of April 1984.  In 1987 the worker was awarded a pension supplement that was continued under s. 135(2) of the pre-1990 Act until October 1990, when it was reduced to a s. 135(4) level.

DecKeywords: Apportionment (negligence); Negligence (res ipsa loquitur); Negligence (standard of care)
DecSummary: A general contractor appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer apportioning 50% of the costs of a compensable accident from the accident employer to it.  The accident employer was a subcontractor on a construction site.  A worker of the subcontractor was injured when some dirt fell in on him in a trench in which he was working.

The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer granting entitlement for a shoulder disability.  The Hearings Officer found that the condition was related to the nature of the worker's work as a hand sewer.

A truck driver suffered chest and low back injuries when he slipped and fell in July 1988.  He returned to modified work in December 1988 but stopped working again due to worsening of his condition.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement subsequent to December 1988.

The worker suffered a low back injury on October 1, 1986, and returned to work on October 27, 1986.  In December 1988, the worker woke up at home with increased back pain.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement in December 1988.

DecKeywords: Adjournment (additional issues); Overpayment (suspension of recovery pending appeal)
DecSummary: The worker was injured in October 1984. He received temporary total benefits from the Board until March 1986, when the Board terminated them on the basis that the worker had refused suitable work that was available at no wage loss.  The worker's objection to that decision was allowed by the Decision Review Specialist and full benefits were restored.  The employer's appeal of that decision was allowed by the Hearings Officer in April 1987.  The Hearings Officer's conclusion that the worker was was not entitled to benefits subsequent to March 1986 resulted in an overpayment of $18,000.  The Tribunal dismissed an appeal from the Hearings Officer's decision.

The worker fractured his right leg in a compensable accident in 1971.  The worker appealed a decision of the Appeal Board denying entitlement for a back condition in 1974 and granting only 50% benefits from December 1972 to January 1973.

DecKeywords: Board Directives and Guidelines (chronic pain); Chronic pain; Pensions (assessment) (chronic pain); Temporary disability (beyond pension level)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a number of compensable accidents.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying temporary benefits from December 1984 to March 1986 while the worker was incarcerated and confirming the worker's 20% pension for chronic pain.  The worker was also appealing a number of other issues but the hearing of these other issues was adjourned at the worker's request.

DecKeywords: Carpal tunnel syndrome; Delay (onset of symptoms)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a shoulder injury in a fall in July 1990.  Several weeks later, the worker began to feel tingling and numbness in his right hand.  The worker's condition was diagnosed as carpal tunnel syndrome.  In December 1990, the worker underwent decompression surgery.  The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer granting entitlement for carpal tunnel syndrome.

DecKeywords: Access to worker file, statutory; Adjournment (representative availability)
DecSummary: The worker was appealing a decision granting access to his file to the employer.  In a preliminary matter, The Panel decided to proceed with the hearing in the unexplained absence of the employer's representative.
The worker suffered an eye injury in November 1990.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying full temporary benefits from August 1991 to September 1991.

A registered nursing assistant appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a severe back condition which the worker related to an incident in January 1984 when she was lifting a patient.  The worker did not claim benefits until 1988.  The worker saw her doctor five days after the incident but did not relate her condition to work.  From the time of the incident until August 1985, the worker saw her doctor 30 times but only mentioned a sore back once.  The worker and her doctor related that at the time to premenstrual syndrome, which had, in the past, caused back pain to the worker.

DecKeywords: Asthma; Delay (onset of symptoms); Exposure (isocyanate fumes)
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for asthma which the worker claimed was caused by exposure to isocyanates in 1970.  Medical literature indicated that asthma could result from exposure to isocyanates.  However, considering delay in onset of recorded symptoms until 1978, the Panel found that the worker's asthma was not related to exposure in 1970.  That exposure may have caused some irritation to his respiratory system but did not cause his asthma.  It was likely that the worker developed adult asthma together with sensitivity to dust.

DecKeywords: Board Directives and Guidelines (hearing loss) (individual susceptibility); Hearing loss; Medical opinion (hearing loss); Preexisting condition (hearing loss)
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for hearing loss.  The noise levels where the worker worked were well below 90 decibels.  However, the worker submitted that his claim should be allowed, considering individual susceptibility.

DecKeywords: Cancer (lung) (squamous cell); Construction (carpenter); Exposure (asbestos); Smoking; Medical opinion (cancer) (lung) (asbestosis)
DecSummary: A construction carpenter appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for squamous cell carcinoma of the upper left lung, which he claimed was related to exposure to asbestos in building materials.

DecKeywords: In the course of employment (off duty); Right to sue; Volunteer; Worker (contract of service) (employment relationship)
DecSummary: The defendants in a civil action applied to determine whether the plaintiffs' rights of action were taken away.  The issue was whether the plaintiffs were workers in the course of employment at the time of a motor vehicle accident.
The appeal was withdrawn after it was determined that there was a second claim file at the Board dealing with the worker's disability.  [3 pages]

The worker suffered a low back injury in February 1989 and received benefits until February 1990.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying further entitlement.  On the evidence, the worker had a preexisting condition from a non-compensable motor vehicle accident.  Her condition had returned to its pre-accident state by February 1990.

The worker suffered a back injury in 1970.  In 1979, he was awarded a pension for his back disability retroactive at the rate of 30% from 1976 and at the rate of 10% from the date of the accident to 1976.  The worker appealed a decision of the Appeals Adjudicator confirming the retroactivity of the pension at only 10% from 1970 to 1976.

DecKeywords: Benefits (review of compensation); Board Directives and Guidelines (earnings basis) (minor); Discretion, Board (earnings basis) (minor); Earnings basis (minor)
DecSummary: The worker, a general journeyman machinist apprentice, suffered a low back injury in 1987, when he was 20 years old.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer regarding the earnings basis for calculation of his 30% pension.  The worker claimed that his benefits should be based on the earnings of a fully qualified general journeyman machinist.

The appeal was adjourned.  Though the Tribunal had jurisdiction in this complex case, the Panel was reluctant to make certain findings because there were still issues before the Board whose resolution may assist the Panel in determining issues arising on this appeal.  [4 pages]

DecKeywords: Suitable employment; Employment (retirement); Supplements, older worker; Supplements, temporary
DecSummary: The worker suffered a back injury in 1981 when he was 53 years old.  He was awarded a 10% pension and received a temporary supplement from 1983 to November 1985.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying a supplement subsequent to November 1985.

The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer granting entitlement for a right knee disability in 1988.  The worker claimed that his condition, diagnosed as chondromalacia, was related to his work as a mechanic on a particular vehicle for a few days before he laid off.

DecKeywords: In the course of employment (travelling); Right to sue

The worker was injured at work, in 1985, when a pry bar that he was using slipped and struck him in the leg.  There was no time lost then.  The worker did not seek professional medical treatment until 1990, when he underwent arthroscopy and a partial medial meniscectomy to his knee.

In Decision No. 865/92, the Tribunal upheld that decision. On reconsideration, the Vice-Chair found that the worker's employment history was a significant contributing factor in the development of the COLD, and that cigarette smoking was also a significant contributing factor. In Decision No. 865/92R4, the Vice-Chair concluded that the Board could not apportion the worker's pension to reflect the contribution of the non-compensable smoking, and that, accordingly, the worker would be entitled to the full amount of the pension, whatever that amount might be.
